topics.title: Document Structure & Syntax
topics.summary: Start from absolute zero: understand what websites, webpages, browsers and HTML files are, then learn tags, elements, attributes, nesting and the small document structure that gives a webpage its meaning.

concepts.name: HTML gives webpage content structure
concepts.explanation: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is a markup language, not a programming language. HTML describes the structure and meaning of webpage content so a browser can understand what is a heading, paragraph, title, link, form control and more.

concepts.name: Elements are built from markup
concepts.explanation: Many HTML elements have an opening tag, some content, and a matching closing tag. For example, <p>Hello</p> is one paragraph element. The angle brackets and slash are part of the markup; they are not meant to appear as ordinary page text.

concepts.name: Elements form a nested document tree
concepts.explanation: HTML elements can contain other elements. This is called nesting. A containing element is often called a parent and an element inside it is a child. Correct nesting and clear indentation make the structure easier for both the browser and the person reading the source code to understand.

beginnerScaffold.learningGoal: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain the difference between a website and a webpage, describe what a browser does with an HTML file, recognize opening and closing tags, build simple elements, add a quoted attribute, nest elements correctly, and create a small complete HTML document with a doctype, html, head, title and body.
beginnerScaffold.whyItMatters: Every webpage needs structure before styling or interactivity can make sense. HTML is the foundation that tells the browser what each piece of content is. If you understand tags, elements, attributes and nesting now, later HTML, CSS and JavaScript lessons become much easier to reason about instead of feeling like collections of mysterious symbols.

terms.meaning: A collection of related webpages and resources that belong together, usually under the same site or domain.
One document or page that a browser can display. A website can contain many webpages.
A program such as Edge, Chrome or Firefox that reads web files, interprets their HTML, and displays the resulting webpage.
HyperText Markup Language. A markup language used to describe the structure and meaning of webpage content.
The text you write and save before the browser interprets it. An HTML source file normally ends with the .html extension.
Special text such as tags and attributes that describes the structure or meaning of content.

Placing one HTML element inside another element.
When one element contains another, the outer element is the parent and the inner element is its child.
Spaces added at the start of nested lines to make the document structure easier for people to read. Indentation usually does not change the meaning of normal HTML.
Information about the document rather than the main visible page content. The head contains metadata such as the page title.

syntax.meaning: The normal filename extension for an HTML document, for example index.html.
Angle brackets mark the beginning and end of an HTML tag.
An opening paragraph tag. It tells the browser that paragraph content begins here.
A closing paragraph tag. The slash / tells the browser that this paragraph element ends here.
Inside a closing tag, the forward slash marks that the element is being closed.
An attribute named lang with the quoted value en. It tells the browser that the content language is English.
Inside an attribute, = connects the attribute name to its value. This is not JavaScript or C# assignment; it is HTML attribute syntax.

The root element that contains the HTML document.
Contains information about the document, such as its title, rather than the main visible page content.
Sets the document title shown by the browser, for example on the tab or window title.
Contains the main content that appears in the webpage.
Marks a top-level heading. Detailed heading hierarchy is taught in Module 2.
A common head element that tells the browser how document text is encoded. meta is a void element, so it does not use a separate closing tag.

recap: A website can contain many webpages; one HTML file commonly represents one webpage/document.
A browser reads HTML source and builds a document structure from its elements and nesting.

pitfalls:
Do not confuse a tag with a complete element.

is an opening tag;

Hello

is a complete paragraph element.
Match closing tags to the element you opened and close nested children before their parent closes.
Keep attribute values quoted in Academy beginner HTML examples so the boundary of the value is obvious.
Do not put visible page content such as headings and paragraphs in head; put main visible content in body.
Do not expect title to create a visible page heading. title describes the document/browser tab; h1 is visible page content.
HTML tag names are not case-sensitive in normal HTML documents, but lowercase is the modern convention used by the Academy. Do not transfer C#/JavaScript case-sensitivity rules blindly to HTML.
A browser may repair malformed HTML. If the preview still displays something after a mistake, inspect your source instead of assuming the markup is correct.

topics.title: Text, Headings & Meaning
topics.summary: Learn how HTML gives written content a clear hierarchy and meaning: use headings for structure, paragraphs for prose, and strong/em only when the text carries importance or stress emphasis.

concepts.name: Headings describe hierarchy
concepts.explanation: Headings are labels for the page and its sections. h1 represents the highest heading level in the structure you are building, followed by h2 for sections beneath it, then h3 for subsections beneath an h2, and so on. Choose heading levels because of structure, not because one happens to look larger or smaller in the browser.

concepts.name: Paragraphs group normal prose
concepts.explanation: The p element marks a paragraph: a block of related sentences or prose. A paragraph is different from a heading. Headings label sections; paragraphs contain the ordinary explanatory text inside those sections.

concepts.name: strong and em add meaning inside text
concepts.explanation: strong marks text that is important, while em marks stress emphasis that can change how a sentence is understood when read aloud. Browsers often display strong as bold and em as italic, but their purpose is meaning. CSS should be used later when the goal is purely visual styling.

beginnerScaffold.learningGoal: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain what headings and paragraphs do, build a logical h1/h2/h3 hierarchy, use p for normal prose, use strong for importance and em for stress emphasis, and choose these elements because of their meaning rather than their default visual appearance.
beginnerScaffold.whyItMatters: A webpage is easier to read and understand when its text has a clear structure. Humans can scan headings to find sections, and browsers and assistive technology can use the same semantic structure to understand how the content is organized. If you choose tags only because they look bold, large or italic, the page may look acceptable while communicating the wrong meaning.

terms.meaning: A short label that introduces the page or a section of content, such as a page title or section title.
The structural level of a heading, written with h1 through h6. Lower numbers represent higher levels in the hierarchy.
An organized parent/subsection relationship. In headings, an h2 can describe a section under an h1, and an h3 can describe a subsection under that h2.
A block of related prose marked with the p element.
Meaning. Semantic HTML uses elements whose names and roles describe what the content actually is, not merely how it should look.
Content that should be treated as especially important. The strong element communicates this meaning.
Emphasis that affects how a word or phrase is stressed when read. The em element communicates this meaning.
Software or hardware that helps people interact with digital content, such as a screen reader. Meaningful HTML structure gives these tools useful information.

syntax.meaning: A level-one heading. In a simple beginner page, this is normally the main heading that names the page or its main topic.
A level-two heading used for a section beneath the higher-level heading.
A level-three heading used for a subsection beneath an h2.
Additional lower heading levels. Intern practice here focuses on h1-h3 so the hierarchy is easy to see, but the full heading range is h1 through h6.
A paragraph element for ordinary prose or related sentences.
Marks text as strongly important. Its common bold appearance is a browser default, not the reason to choose the element.
Marks stress emphasis. Its common italic appearance is a browser default, not the reason to choose the element.

examples.title: Step 2 — Put ordinary prose in a paragraph

Do not choose strong only to get bold text or em only to get italic text. Use them when the content actually has importance or stress emphasis.

Remember that browsers may repair malformed paragraph or heading markup; visible output alone does not prove your source hierarchy is correct.

topics.title: Links, Images & Lists
topics.summary: Learn how webpages connect to other resources, how images are embedded with useful text alternatives, and how related items are grouped into unordered or ordered lists.

concepts.name: Links connect one resource to another
concepts.explanation: The a element creates a hyperlink. Its href attribute tells the browser where the link should go, while the text between and is what the learner sees and activates. Good link text should describe the destination instead of using vague wording such as only 'click here'.

concepts.name: Images need both a source and a text alternative
concepts.explanation: The img element embeds an image. src tells the browser where the image file is, and alt provides text that communicates the image's meaning or purpose when the image cannot be seen. img is a void element, so it does not wrap content with a separate closing tag.

concepts.name: Lists group related items
concepts.explanation: ul creates an unordered list when the order is not important, ol creates an ordered list when sequence or ranking matters, and li marks each individual list item. The li elements belong inside the ul or ol that groups them.

beginnerScaffold.learningGoal: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to create a useful link, explain what href does, recognize the difference between a simple relative destination and a full web address, add an image with src and meaningful alt text, build unordered and ordered lists with li items, and combine links, images and lists without using concepts that have not been taught yet.
beginnerScaffold.whyItMatters: Real webpages rarely contain only headings and paragraphs. They connect people to other pages, show useful images, and organize related information into lists. These structures are also building blocks for navigation, galleries, menus and content cards that you will meet later, so understanding their basic HTML now gives you a dependable foundation.

terms.meaning: A piece of content that can take the user to another page, file, location or web resource.
The place a link points to, such as another HTML file or a full website address.
A web address. A full URL can look like https://example.com/guide.
A destination written relative to the current file, such as lessons.html. The browser looks for that resource based on where the current page is stored.
An image file that the browser can load, such as academy-badge.png.
Text that communicates an image's meaning or purpose when the image is unavailable or cannot be perceived visually.
A list whose items belong together but do not need a numbered sequence.
A list where sequence, steps or ranking matters.
One entry inside an unordered or ordered list.

syntax.meaning: The anchor element used to create a hyperlink. The content between the tags becomes the visible link text.
The href attribute gives the anchor its destination. Here the destination is a relative HTML file named lessons.html.
An href can also contain a full web address beginning with a scheme such as https://.
The image element embeds an image resource. img is a void element, so it does not use a separate </img> closing tag.
The src attribute tells the browser which image resource to load.
The alt attribute provides a text alternative that describes the image's useful meaning or purpose.
An empty alt value can be used for a purely decorative image so it does not add unnecessary information. You only need to recognize this idea in Intern; the practice uses meaningful alt text.
Creates an unordered list when the items belong together but their order is not important.
Creates an ordered list when sequence, priority or ranking matters.
Creates one list item inside a ul or ol.

examples.title: Step 1 — Create one link
examples.explanation: The a element wraps the visible link text. href is an attribute on the opening tag and tells the browser where to go when the link is activated.

examples.title: Step 4 — Add one image
examples.explanation: img does not wrap text, so it has no separate closing tag. src names the image resource and alt provides a useful text alternative.

examples.title: Step 5 — Build an unordered list
examples.explanation: Use ul when the items are related but their order does not matter. Each entry is placed inside its own li element.

examples.title: Step 6 — Build an ordered list
examples.explanation: Use ol when the order itself carries meaning, such as a short sequence of steps.

When the user activates the link, the browser tries to navigate to the resource named by href.
For img, the browser reads src and requests that image resource. If the resource cannot be loaded, the image may appear broken, but the HTML element still exists.
The alt value becomes the image's text alternative. It is not a caption that automatically appears below the image.
For ul or ol, the browser builds a list container and then places each li child inside that list structure.
Browsers may still display malformed list or link markup after repairing it, so inspect the source structure rather than trusting appearance alone.

errorExamples.explanation: HTML can allow some unquoted attribute values, but omitting quotes makes beginner source harder to read and becomes fragile when values contain characters that require quoting.
errorExamples.fix: Use the Academy beginner style: href="lessons.html".

errorExamples.explanation: The markup works, but the link text does not explain what destination the user will get.
errorExamples.fix: Use descriptive text such as Read the lessons.

errorExamples.explanation: The image has a source but no alt attribute, so its useful meaning is not provided as a text alternative.
errorExamples.fix: Add meaningful alt text, for example alt="Code Ascension Academy badge".

errorExamples.explanation: The alt text is technically present but 'image' does not communicate what the image means or does.
errorExamples.fix: Describe the useful information or purpose, for example alt="Code Ascension Academy badge".

errorExamples.explanation: img is a void element in HTML. It does not wrap content and does not use a separate </img> closing tag.
errorExamples.fix: Write only .

recap: a creates a hyperlink; href gives the destination and the content between the tags is the visible link text.
Use descriptive link text so the purpose makes sense without vague wording such as only 'click here'.
A relative destination such as lessons.html refers to a resource based on the current page's location; a full https:// URL can point elsewhere on the web.
img embeds an image; src identifies the resource and alt provides its text alternative.
img is a void element and does not use a separate closing tag.
ul groups items when order is not important; ol groups items when sequence or ranking matters.
Each list entry belongs in an li element inside its ul or ol container.
Links can be placed inside list items because HTML elements can be nested.
Do not assume a resource path is correct just because the HTML syntax is valid; a wrong href or src can still point to something that does not exist.

topics.title: Forms & Basic Controls
topics.summary: Learn what a web form is and build simple, understandable controls with labels, text and email inputs, names, required fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, and an explicit submit button.

concepts.name: Forms collect related user input
concepts.explanation: A form groups controls that ask the user for information or choices. At Intern level, focus on the structure of the controls and their labels. Sending form data to a server is a later topic.

concepts.name: Labels explain controls
concepts.explanation: A label tells the user what an input is for. Connecting label for="..." to the matching input id="..." makes the relationship explicit and also lets the user click the label to focus or toggle the control.

concepts.name: Input type changes the control's job
concepts.explanation: The input element can represent different controls. type="text" accepts normal text, type="email" asks for an email-shaped value, type="checkbox" represents an independent yes/no choice, and type="radio" represents one choice inside a group.

beginnerScaffold.learningGoal: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain what a form and form control are, connect a label to an input, create text and email inputs, explain the different jobs of id and name, add the required attribute, recognize basic checkbox and radio controls, and build a small form with an explicit submit button.
beginnerScaffold.whyItMatters: Forms are how webpages ask people for information and choices. Login screens, search boxes, profile editors, checkout pages and settings screens all build on the same basic ideas. Learning the native HTML controls first gives you working keyboard behavior and useful browser features before CSS or JavaScript is added.

terms.meaning: A container that groups controls which belong to one user-input task.
An interactive element used to enter or choose information, such as an input or button.
Text that names or explains a form control. A label should be connected to the control it describes.
A void HTML element used for several kinds of user input. Its type attribute changes what kind of control it becomes.
An input that accepts a short piece of normal text, commonly created with type="text".
An input created with type="email". The browser can check that a supplied value has a basic email-like shape.
An identifier for one element in the page. In this lesson it lets a label point to its matching input.
A label attribute whose value should match the id of the control the label describes.
A form-control name used to identify that piece of data when form data is eventually collected or submitted.
A boolean HTML attribute that tells the browser the control must have an acceptable value before ordinary form submission is allowed.
A control for an independent on/off or yes/no choice. Multiple checkboxes can normally be selected independently.
A control for choosing one option from a group. Radio buttons belong to the same group when they share the same name.
A button whose type is submit. Activating it asks the form to submit, after browser validation rules such as required have been checked.
Built-in checks the browser can perform, such as noticing an empty required field or a badly shaped email value. These checks help the user but are not a replacement for later server-side validation.

syntax.meaning: Group controls that belong to the same form task. This Intern lesson does not require action or method yet.
Create a visible label and connect it to the element whose id is display-name.
Create an input control. input is a void element, so it does not use a separate </input> closing tag.
Give this element an identifier. The matching label can point to it with for="display-name".
Give the input's data a name. id connects page relationships; name identifies the form value.
Create a normal short text input.
Create an input intended for an email address and enable basic browser email-format checking.
A boolean attribute. Its presence turns the requirement on; you do not need to write required="true".
Create an independent checkable choice.
Create one option in a radio group. Radio inputs in the same group share the same name.
Give a checkbox/radio choice a data value that represents the option when form data is later collected.
Create an explicit submit button. Writing the type makes the button's job clear.

examples.title: Step 1 — Create an empty form container
examples.explanation: The form element groups controls that belong to one input task. At this stage it does not need to send anything anywhere.

examples.title: Step 2 — Add one visible label
examples.explanation: A label gives the user a human-readable description. It becomes much more useful once it is connected to its input in the next step.

examples.title: Step 3 — Add a text input and connect the label
examples.explanation: The label's for value and the input's id value are identical. That creates the label-control relationship. type="text" makes a normal text field.

examples.title: Step 4 — Give the form value a name
examples.explanation: name is not the same job as id. id helps identify the element in the page; name identifies the piece of form data.

examples.title: Step 5 — Require a value
examples.explanation: required is a boolean attribute. If the user tries normal submission while the field is empty, the browser can stop the submission and ask for a value.
examples.code:
<label for="display-name">Display name</label>
<input id="display-name" name="displayName" type="text" required>

examples.title: Step 6 — Add an email field
examples.explanation: The structure is the same, but type="email" tells the browser the value should look like an email address. This is basic browser validation, not proof that the address belongs to the user.

examples.title: Step 7 — See a checkbox choice
examples.explanation: A checkbox represents an independent choice. Clicking the connected label also toggles the checkbox. This example is for recognition and practice; the final Module 4 task does not require a checkbox.
examples.code:
<input id="reminders" name="reminders" type="checkbox">
<label for="reminders">Send study reminders</label>

examples.title: Step 8 — See a radio-button group
examples.explanation: Both radio inputs use name="studyMode", so the browser treats them as one group where only one option is normally selected at a time. Each input has its own id so each label points to the correct option.
examples.code:
<input id="guided" name="studyMode" type="radio" value="guided">
<label for="guided">Guided</label>

<input id="solo" name="studyMode" type="radio" value="solo">
<label for="solo">Solo</label>

examples.title: Step 9 — Add an explicit submit button
examples.explanation: A submit button asks the form to submit. Before ordinary submission, the browser checks built-in rules such as required and the basic format expected by type="email".

examples.title: Step 10 — Combine the required Module 4 pieces
examples.explanation: The final beginner form uses two correctly labelled inputs with names, text/email types, required validation, and one explicit submit button. Server destination details are intentionally left for a later lesson.
examples.code:
<form>
  <label for="display-name">Display name</label>
  <input id="display-name" name="displayName" type="text" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Save profile</button>
</form>

breakdown.meaning: Begin the group of related controls.
Begin a label whose for value points to the input with id display-name.
The human-readable label text shown to the user.
Identify this particular input so its label can reference it.
Name this piece of form data for when data is later collected/submitted.
Make this input a normal text field.
Ask the browser not to allow ordinary submission while this required control has no acceptable value.
Make this input an email field with basic browser email-shape validation.
Create a button whose explicit job is to submit the form.
End the form after all of its controls.

computerSteps: The browser parses the form and creates native interactive controls for each input and button.
For each label with a for value, the browser looks for the control whose id matches that value and connects them.
The browser uses each input type to decide what control behavior and basic validation should apply.
The name attribute identifies each control's data value for later form-data collection; it is a different job from id.
When the user activates the submit button, the browser first checks built-in constraints such as required and the basic format of an email input.
Because this Intern lesson does not configure a server destination, focus on the form structure and validation behavior rather than real data delivery.
guidedChanges: Change the visible label text from Display name to Learner name without changing for or id. Explain why the connection still works.
Change both for="display-name" and id="display-name" to for="learner-name" and id="learner-name". Keep the two values matching.
Temporarily make the label's for value different from the input's id, then restore them. Notice why matching identifiers matter.
Remove required from one input and explain which browser requirement you removed.
Change a type="text" field to type="email" and explain what extra expectation the browser now has for the value.
Add the checkbox example for study reminders and test clicking its label to toggle it.
Add the two radio examples with the same name, then change one radio's name and observe why they no longer behave as one group.
Change the submit button's visible text without changing type="submit". Explain which part changes appearance and which part defines behavior.
beginnerScaffold.workedExampleIntro: This worked example uses only the required Module 4 foundation: a form container, two labels connected with for/id, text and email inputs with names and required validation, and one explicit submit button. Checkbox/radio controls are introduced for recognition but are not required in the final practice. action, method, server handling, JavaScript form events, select, textarea and advanced validation remain later topics.

errorExamples.explanation: The label is visible but it is not explicitly connected to the input because it has no for attribute.
errorExamples.fix: Use <label for="display-name">Display name</label> with id="display-name" on the input.

errorExamples.explanation: The label points to id name, but the input's id is display-name. The values do not match.
errorExamples.fix: Make for and id identical, for example for="display-name" and id="display-name".

errorExamples.explanation: The input can still exist, but it has no name. Without a name, this value will not have the expected form-data key when data is later collected or submitted.
errorExamples.fix: Add a meaningful name such as name="email".

errorExamples.explanation: This accepts text, but it does not tell the browser that the value is intended to be an email address.
errorExamples.fix: Use type="email" for this email field.

errorExamples.explanation: required is a boolean attribute. In HTML, merely having the required attribute present turns the requirement on; the text value "false" does not switch it off.
errorExamples.fix: Remove the required attribute when the field should be optional, or write just required when it should be required.

errorExamples.explanation: input is a void element. It does not wrap content and does not use a separate closing </input> tag.
errorExamples.fix: Use only <input type="text">.

errorExamples.mistake:
<input id="guided" name="guided" type="radio">
<input id="solo" name="solo" type="radio">
errorExamples.explanation: These radio buttons use different names, so the browser treats them as different groups and both may be selected.
errorExamples.fix: Give options in one group the same name, for example name="studyMode".

errorExamples.explanation: Inside a form, a button without an explicit type commonly behaves as a submit button. That can be surprising while learning.
errorExamples.fix: Write the intended behavior explicitly: <button type="submit">Save profile</button>.

errorExamples.mistake: type="email" means the email address is real and safe
errorExamples.explanation: The browser only performs basic format checks. It cannot prove that the address exists, belongs to the user, or that submitted data is trustworthy.
errorExamples.fix: Treat browser validation as helpful user feedback. Real applications also validate data in trusted application/server code, which is a later topic.

recap: A form groups controls that belong to one user-input task.
A label explains a control; for on the label should match id on the control.
id identifies the page element, while name identifies the form-data value.
input is a void element whose type changes the control's job.
type="text" creates normal text input; type="email" adds a basic email-format expectation.
required is a boolean attribute whose presence enables a browser requirement.
Checkboxes are independent choices; radio buttons form a one-choice group when they share a name.
An explicit <button type="submit"> makes the button's job clear.
Browser validation helps users but does not replace later trusted validation.
Intern Module 4 focuses on form structure; action, method, server processing and JavaScript form logic are intentionally deferred.

topics.example:
<form>
  <label for="display-name">Display name</label>
  <input id="display-name" name="displayName" type="text" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Save profile</button>
</form>

Connect each label with for/id, give each input a name, make both fields required, and use type="email" for the email field. Do not add action, method, JavaScript or server code yet.
topics.hint: Build one control at a time. For each field, make label for and input id match; then add name, type and required. Finish with <button type="submit">.

  <input id="display-name" name="displayName" type="text" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Save profile</button>

testCodeQuestions.prompt: Create one labelled text input for a learner name. Connect label for to the input id, give the input a name, use type="text", and make it required.
Create a small form containing one labelled required email input plus an explicit submit button. Use name on the input, type="email", and type="submit" on the button.

examPrompts.2: Exam 2: Build a form with one labelled required email input and one explicit submit button. Include name, type="email", and type="submit".

pitfalls: Do not rely on visible label text alone; connect label for to the matching input id.
Do not confuse id with name. id identifies an element in the page; name identifies the form-data value.
Use type="email" when the control is meant for an email address instead of using a generic text input without explanation.
Remember that required is a boolean attribute: required="false" still leaves the attribute present and therefore enabled.
Remember that input is a void element and does not use </input>.
Radio options that belong to one group should share the same name; each option can still have its own id/value.
Write button type explicitly while learning so its behavior is not accidental.
Do not mistake browser validation for trusted application/server validation.
Do not add action, method, JavaScript handlers or advanced controls just to complete Module 4; they have not been required yet.
mastery: Explain what a form and a form control are in your own words.
Create a label/input pair and explain how for and id connect them.
Explain the different jobs of id and name.
Create text and email inputs and explain why their type values differ.
Explain how the required boolean attribute behaves.
Recognize input as a void element and avoid writing </input>.
Explain the basic difference between an independent checkbox and a radio-button group.
Explain why radio buttons in one group share a name.

topics.title: Semantic Page Structure & Accessibility Basics
topics.summary: Learn how semantic HTML gives a page meaningful regions and reading structure, then apply beginner accessibility habits using native elements, logical headings, descriptive content, and clean source order.

concepts.name: Semantic elements describe the job of a region
concepts.explanation: A semantic HTML element tells the browser and other tools something about what its content represents. Instead of treating every block as an unnamed container, elements such as header, nav, main and footer communicate purpose. The goal is meaningful structure, not a different visual style.

concepts.name: Sections and articles organize main content
concepts.explanation: section groups a themed part of a page and normally has a heading that names that theme. article represents self-contained content that could make sense on its own, such as a news story, forum post, lesson card or blog entry. Not every group of elements needs to become a section or article.

concepts.name: Accessible HTML starts with the native structure
concepts.explanation: Good accessibility begins with the HTML you already know: logical headings, descriptive links, useful image alt text, connected form labels, and native semantic regions. Assistive technology can use that structure. ARIA can be useful later, but it should not replace correct native HTML.

topics.starter:
Code Ascension Academy

Current path

I am learning semantic HTML.

beginnerScaffold.learningGoal: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain what semantic HTML and accessibility mean at a beginner level, identify the jobs of header, nav, main, section, article and footer, build a page whose source order and heading hierarchy make sense, and explain why native HTML should come before unnecessary ARIA.
beginnerScaffold.whyItMatters: A webpage is not only something people look at. People may navigate it with a keyboard, hear it through a screen reader, zoom it heavily, restyle it, or consume it through other software. Meaningful HTML gives all of those experiences a stronger structure before CSS and JavaScript are involved.

terms.meaning: HTML chosen because an element describes the meaning or job of its content, not merely because of how the browser happens to display it.
Designing content so people with different abilities and ways of using a computer can perceive, understand, navigate and operate it.
Software or hardware that helps a person interact with digital content. A screen reader is one example.
Software that can present interface and webpage information through speech or other non-visual output.
A meaningful page region that helps describe the page structure. Native elements such as nav and main can provide landmark information.
Introductory content for a page or a section. In this Intern lesson we use header for the page introduction.
A group of important links used to move to major destinations. HTML represents this with nav.
The primary content of the page. HTML represents it with main; a normal page should not have several competing visible main regions.
A themed grouping of content, normally with a heading that tells the reader what the section is about.
Self-contained content that can still make sense as an individual item, such as a lesson update, post, or story.
Closing or supporting information for a page or section. In this lesson we use footer for page-level closing information.
The order elements appear in the HTML source. A sensible source order should tell a coherent story even before visual layout is added.
A set of accessibility attributes used when extra accessibility information is genuinely needed. It is not a replacement for correct native HTML.

syntax.meaning: Wrap introductory page content such as the page heading.
Wrap a major group of navigation links. Do not use nav for every random link on the page.
Wrap the page's primary content. Keep one clear visible main region in a normal beginner page.
Group content about one theme. Give the section a meaningful heading when it needs a named place in the document structure.
Wrap self-contained content that could reasonably stand as an individual item.
Wrap closing or supporting information. This lesson uses it as the page footer.
Keep heading levels connected to the content hierarchy you learned in Module 2.
Prefer the correct built-in element and attributes you already know before reaching for extra accessibility attributes.

examples.title: Step 1 — Give the page an introductory header
examples.explanation: The header groups the page introduction. The h1 still provides the actual top-level heading; header does not replace headings.

examples.title: Step 2 — Mark the primary content with main
examples.explanation: main identifies the content that is central to this page. It is not a styling box and it does not automatically create a heading, so the content inside still needs its own logical headings.

examples.title: Step 3 — Put major navigation links inside nav
examples.explanation: nav is for an important navigation group. The links themselves are the same a elements you learned in Module 3. A short list gives the links a clear grouped structure.

examples.title: Step 4 — Create a named section
examples.explanation: section groups content about one theme. The h2 tells the reader what this section is about. A section is not just a generic wrapper for spacing.
examples.code:
Current path

I am working through HTML Intern.

examples.title: Step 5 — Recognize self-contained article content
examples.explanation: This lesson update can make sense as one self-contained item, so article is meaningful. Its h3 fits beneath the h2 of the surrounding section.

examples.title: Step 6 — Add closing information with footer
examples.explanation: A page footer can contain closing or supporting information. The footer element adds meaning; it does not force the footer to the bottom of the screen or style it automatically.

examples.title: Step 7 — Check the source order before thinking about CSS
examples.explanation: Read the elements from top to bottom: introduction, navigation, primary content, closing information. If that order makes sense without visual layout, you have a strong structural starting point.

examples.title: Step 8 — Reuse the accessibility habits you already learned
examples.explanation: Semantic regions do not replace the earlier rules. Keep headings logical, links descriptive, image alt text meaningful, and form labels connected. Accessibility is built from these small correct choices working together.

examples.title: Step 9 — Know when not to add ARIA
examples.explanation: The native nav element already communicates navigation semantics. At Intern level, do not add roles or ARIA attributes simply because they sound more accessible. Learn the native structure first; later ranks can cover cases where extra accessible naming or roles are genuinely needed.

examples.explanation: The final structure uses only native elements and concepts taught across HTML Intern. The headings follow h1 → h2 → h3, navigation reuses normal links, and the page still makes sense if styling is removed.

breakdown.meaning: Introduces the page; it does not replace the h1 inside it.
Groups important navigation links that move the learner to major destinations.
Marks the primary page content and gives the page one clear central region.
Creates a themed region and names that theme with a heading.
Creates one self-contained content item inside the broader section.
Provides page-level closing/supporting information.
Preserves the content hierarchy rather than choosing heading numbers for visual size.
Continues the Module 3 habit of describing where a link goes rather than using vague text.

computerSteps: The browser parses the HTML from top to bottom and builds its document structure from the nested elements.
Native semantic elements contribute meaning to that structure; they are not merely visual containers.
Assistive technology can use headings and landmark information to help a person understand or move around the page.
The browser still renders the content even if no CSS exists, which is why meaningful source order matters.
If markup is malformed, the browser may repair it. Inspect the source structure rather than judging correctness only by appearance.

beginnerScaffold.workedExampleIntro: This final HTML Intern example combines concepts from all five modules. Focus on meaning first: introduction, navigation, primary content, themed section, self-contained article, then closing information. Notice that no ARIA is required to make these native elements semantic.

errorExamples.mistake:
Lessons
used as the only navigation structure
errorExamples.explanation: A generic div does not communicate that the content is a navigation region.
errorExamples.fix: Use <nav> around the major navigation links when the content really is navigation.

errorExamples.mistake: Two separate visible <main> regions competing as primary content
errorExamples.explanation: A normal page should have one clear primary main region. Multiple visible main regions make the page structure ambiguous.
errorExamples.fix: Keep one main for the page's primary content and use section/article for structure inside it.

errorExamples.mistake:
...

with no reason or identifiable theme
errorExamples.explanation: section is semantic, not a generic styling wrapper. A thematic section normally benefits from a heading that identifies its topic.
errorExamples.fix: Give the section a meaningful heading, or use a non-semantic container later if there is no semantic section to describe.

errorExamples.explanation: article is intended for self-contained content, not every block of text.
errorExamples.fix: Use p for normal prose; use article when the whole content item can reasonably stand on its own.

errorExamples.mistake:
Page

followed by

Current path

for a direct section
errorExamples.explanation: The heading number was chosen without following the content hierarchy.
errorExamples.fix: Use the logical next level, such as h2 for a direct section beneath the page h1.

errorExamples.explanation: The semantic nav region is present, but the link text is still vague. Accessibility depends on the smaller content choices too.
errorExamples.fix: Use descriptive text such as HTML lessons.

errorExamples.explanation: Semantic page regions do not remove the need for meaningful text alternatives on informative images.
errorExamples.fix: Add appropriate alt text, for example alt="Code Ascension Academy badge".

errorExamples.mistake: <input id="email" type="email"> with an unrelated or missing label
errorExamples.explanation: Adding semantic landmarks does not repair inaccessible form controls.
errorExamples.fix: Keep the Module 4 label relationship: <label for="email">Email</label> with id="email".

errorExamples.mistake: Adding role="navigation" to <nav> only because “more accessibility attributes must be better”
errorExamples.explanation: The native nav element already carries navigation semantics. Redundant ARIA is not the beginner goal.
errorExamples.fix: Use the correct native element first. Add ARIA later only when there is a real accessibility need you understand.

errorExamples.mistake: Moving content into a strange source order only to achieve a visual layout
errorExamples.explanation: People and tools may encounter the source/reading order differently from a visual CSS layout.
errorExamples.fix: Keep the HTML order logical, then use CSS later to create presentation without destroying the content story.

recap: Semantic HTML describes what content is for, not how large, colorful or positioned it should look.
header introduces, nav groups major navigation, main contains primary content, and footer closes/supports the page.
section groups a theme; article is a self-contained content item.
Heading hierarchy and source order remain important inside semantic regions.
Accessibility builds on native elements plus the link, alt-text and label habits learned earlier.
ARIA is a later tool for real gaps; it is not a replacement for correct HTML.

pitfalls: Do not choose semantic elements because of their default appearance. Their purpose is meaning; CSS controls presentation later.
Do not use nav for every link. Reserve it for an important navigation group.
Keep one clear visible main region for a normal beginner page rather than creating several competing primary-content regions.
Do not use section merely as a generic wrapper. A semantic section should represent a real theme and normally has a heading.
Do not use article for every paragraph or card-shaped box. Use it when the content item is meaningfully self-contained.
Keep heading levels tied to structure, not visual size, even inside header/section/article elements.
Semantic landmarks do not replace descriptive link text, useful image alt text or connected form labels.
Do not assume adding more ARIA automatically creates better accessibility. Prefer correct native HTML first.
Keep source order understandable before using CSS to change the visual layout.
Remember that browsers may repair malformed nesting, so inspect the source instead of trusting appearance alone.
mastery: Explain semantic HTML in your own words and distinguish meaning from visual styling.
Explain the beginner-level jobs of header, nav, main and footer.
Explain the difference between section and article using your own example.
Build a page with one h1 and logical h2/h3 headings inside semantic regions.
Explain why a normal page should have one clear visible main region.
Explain why nav should contain major navigation rather than every link on a page.
Read a page fragment from top to bottom and judge whether its source order tells a coherent story.
Reuse descriptive link text, alt text and form-label habits from Modules 3–4 when those elements appear inside semantic regions.
Explain why native HTML should be preferred before adding unnecessary ARIA.
Build the Module 5 practice without relying on CSS, JavaScript, advanced ARIA, custom roles, or concepts from later HTML ranks.
